quote: Beweisen, dass man durch eine endliche Anzahl von Operationen entscheiden kann, ob und wie viele ganzzahlige Lösungen $\varphi(x,y,..)=0$ mit ganzzahligen Coeffizienten besteht.
english: Prove that one can decide by a finite number of operations whether, and how many, integer solutions $\varphi(x,y,..)=0$ with integer coefficients has.
topic: Miscellaneous notes: a bound on the number of pairwise commuting infinitesimal projective transformations, a question on real roots of the hypergeometric function, a scheme for a space curve, a decision problem for integer solutions of Diophantine equations, and literature for a course on descriptive geometry.

triage.modern_statement: Is there an algorithm that takes any polynomial φ(x1,…,xn) with integer coefficients and decides, in finitely many steps, whether φ = 0 has a solution in integers? Hilbert's note also asks the algorithm to find how many solutions there are (for example, finitely or infinitely many). This is Hilbert's Tenth Problem.
triage.answered_by: The answer is no: no such algorithm can exist. This was completed by Yuri Matiyasevich in 1970, building on about 21 years of work by Martin Davis, Hilary Putnam and Julia Robinson (the MRDP / DPRM theorem). The note is in substance problem 10 of Hilbert's 23 problems, presented at the 1900 Paris International Congress of Mathematicians (ICM).

evidence.claim: Hilbert's tenth problem has a negative solution: no general algorithm can exist. The result came from 21 years of combined work by Davis, Matiyasevich, Putnam and Robinson, and Matiyasevich completed it in 1970.

The problem asks for an algorithm that decides whether a multivariate polynomial equation with integer coefficients has a solution in Z. Matiyasevich (1970) proved that no such algorithm exists, based on work by Putnam, Robinson and Davis.
An important generalization, Hilbert's 10th problem over Q, is still open.
Hilbert's Tenth Problem over Q (whether solvability in rationals is decidable) is listed as an open problem.

triage.why: The diary entry matches the wording of problem 10 from Hilbert's 1900 list: deciding 'by a finite number of operations' whether an integer-coefficient Diophantine equation has integer solutions. The original question over Z was settled negatively in 1970 (Matiyasevich, after Davis–Putnam–Robinson). The extra 'how many' part is also undecidable, because deciding whether solutions exist at all is already impossible. Related questions remain an active research area, especially the version over the rationals Q (still open, per the arXiv survey and the open-problem listing) and versions over rings of integers of number fields. The Wikipedia article also discusses ongoing work on how far the degree and number of unknowns can be reduced while keeping the problem undecidable.
